title: Testing: Swift Testing, XCTest & UI Tests
scopeHtml: Scope: Swift Testing framework, XCTest, async tests, mocks and fakes, snapshot tests, XCUITest, test plans, coverage, CI.

notes.title: Baseline and the iOS testing landscape
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. On Android you write local unit tests with JUnit + MockK + Turbine, instrumented tests with Espresso or the Compose test rule, and run them via Gradle on CI. On iOS you write tests with Swift Testing (new) or XCTest (old), UI tests with XCUITest, and run them via Xcode or xcodebuild test.

Baseline. Swift 6 language mode, Xcode 16+, iOS 17/18 minimum, SwiftUI-first. Swift Testing (import Testing, @Test, #expect) is the default for unit tests; XCTest remains required for UI tests and performance tests and is what you will meet in old codebases. Anything new in Xcode 16/26: verify.

              +------------------+
              |   XCUITest (few) |  slow, real app process, accessibility based
              +------------------+
          +--------------------------+
          | Integration (some)       |  real view model + fake network (URLProtocol)
          +--------------------------+
     +--------------------------------------+
     | Unit tests (many): Swift Testing     |  pure logic, protocol fakes, fast
     +--------------------------------------+
Android iOS
JUnit 4/5 Swift Testing (@Test) / XCTest (XCTestCase)
assertEquals #expect(a == b) / XCTAssertEqual
MockK / Mockito hand-written fakes (no runtime mocking in Swift)
Turbine for Flow AsyncStream collection / confirmation
Espresso / Compose onNodeWithTag XCUITest queries with accessibility identifiers
Paparazzi / Roborazzi swift-snapshot-testing (Point-Free)
Gradle test tasks / Jacoco xcodebuild test, test plans, Xcode code coverage
Robolectric no real equivalent (iOS unit tests run on the Simulator, fast enough)

Targets. A unit test bundle (MyAppTests) is hosted either inside the app process (host application) or as a logic test with no host. UI tests (MyAppUITests) launch the app as a separate process and drive it from outside. This is why UI tests cannot touch your internal types.

Real industry examples. Airbnb, Lyft and Uber publish heavy use of snapshot and UI tests; Point-Free's Swift Composable Architecture ships TestStore for exhaustive state testing. Apple's own sample projects migrated to Swift Testing from WWDC24.

Everyday analogy. The pyramid is a restaurant kitchen: tasting each ingredient (unit), tasting a sauce combination (integration), and occasionally a full dinner service rehearsal (UI) that takes hours.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying iOS has Mockito-style mocking. Swift has no reflection-based proxy generation; you write fakes or use macro/codegen libraries (Mockolo, swift-mocks, verify current options).
  • Believing UI tests can call app internals; they run in a separate process.
  • Calling XCTest obsolete; UI and performance tests still need it.

notes.title: Swift Testing basics: @Test, #expect, #require
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In JUnit you annotate @Test and use assertion functions. In Swift Testing you annotate functions with @Test, group them in a struct (or @Suite), and write plain Swift boolean expressions inside #expect(...). Macros capture the expression and show you each sub-value on failure.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
import Testing
@testable import MyApp

struct PriceCalculatorTests {
    let calc = PriceCalculator(taxRate: 0.1)

    @Test func addsTax() {
        #expect(calc.total(for: 100) == 110)
    }

    @Test("rejects negative prices") func negative() throws {
        #expect(throws: PriceError.negative) {
            try calc.validate(-1)
        }
    }

    @Test func parsesFirstItem() throws {
        let items = try #require(calc.parse("a,b"))   // stops the test if nil
        #expect(items.first == "a")
    }
}
class PriceCalculatorTest {
    private val calc = PriceCalculator(taxRate = 0.1)

    @Test fun addsTax() {
        assertEquals(110, calc.total(100))
    }

    @Test fun negative() {
        assertThrows<PriceError.Negative> { calc.validate(-1) }
    }

    @Test fun parsesFirstItem() {
        val items = requireNotNull(calc.parse("a,b"))
        assertEquals("a", items.first())
    }
}

Key differences from XCTest.

  • Suites are structs/actors/classes and a fresh instance is created per test, so stored properties act as setUp and init()/deinit replace setUp/tearDown. Prefer a struct (value type, no shared state).
  • #expect does not stop the test on failure (it records an issue and continues). #require throws and stops, like a failed precondition. Use #require to unwrap optionals.
  • Expressions: #expect(a == b), #expect(list.isEmpty), #expect(throws: SomeError.self) { ... }, #expect(throws: Never.self) (asserts no throw). On failure you see the evaluated sub-expressions.
  • Display names: @Test("readable name").
  • Issues: Issue.record("message") replaces XCTFail.

Traits modify tests declaratively:

import Testing

@Suite("Network layer", .tags(.networking))
struct NetworkTests {
    @Test(.disabled("flaky upstream, tracked in TICKET-12")) func a() {}

    @Test(.enabled(if: ProcessInfo.processInfo.environment["CI"] != nil)) func b() {}

    @Test(.timeLimit(.minutes(1))) func c() async {}

    @Test(.bug("https://example.com/ticket/99", "crashes on empty")) func d() {}

    @available(iOS 18, *) @Test func e() {}
}

extension Tag { @Tag static var networking: Self }

Available traits (confirm exact spellings per Xcode version: verify): .tags, .disabled, .enabled(if:), .timeLimit, .bug, .serialized, .comment. Tests run in parallel by default (in-process, using Swift concurrency), whereas XCTest runs serially in-process unless you enable parallel simulators. .serialized forces ordering within a suite.

Parameterized tests. One test, many inputs, each reported separately (Android: JUnit5 @ParameterizedTest).

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
@Test("tax by region", arguments: [
    ("IN", 18), ("DE", 19), ("US", 7)
])
func tax(region: String, expectedPercent: Int) {
    #expect(TaxTable.percent(for: region) == expectedPercent)
}

@Test(arguments: [1, 2, 3], ["a", "b"])   // cartesian product: 6 cases
func combos(n: Int, s: String) { /* ... */ }
@ParameterizedTest
@CsvSource("IN,18", "DE,19", "US,7")
fun tax(region: String, expectedPercent: Int) {
    assertEquals(expectedPercent, TaxTable.percent(region))
}

Pass zip(a, b) to avoid the cartesian product. Arguments must be Sendable. A single failing argument can be re-run alone from the Xcode test navigator.

Interop. Swift Testing and XCTest coexist in one target; do not mix assertion APIs inside one test (XCTAssert inside @Test is unsupported, verify).

Real industry examples. Apple's swift-format and swift-collections moved to Swift Testing; Point-Free's libraries support both.

Everyday analogy. XCTest is a printed form with fixed boxes; Swift Testing is a notebook where you write the claim in your own words and the system shows you exactly which part of the sentence was false.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting setUp to share state across tests. Each test gets a new suite instance.
  • Using #expect on an optional unwrap and then dereferencing; use #require.
  • Forgetting that tests run in parallel and sharing mutable global state (singletons, UserDefaults.standard).
  • Saying Swift Testing can do UI or performance (measure) tests. It cannot; use XCTest.

notes.title: XCTest and migrating from it
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. XCTest is the JUnit 4 of iOS: a class per test case, methods starting with test, assertion functions and lifecycle hooks. You will meet it in nearly every old codebase.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
import XCTest
@testable import MyApp

final class PriceCalculatorXCTests: XCTestCase {
    var calc: PriceCalculator!

    override func setUp() {
        super.setUp()
        calc = PriceCalculator(taxRate: 0.1)
    }

    override func tearDown() {
        calc = nil
        super.tearDown()
    }

    func testAddsTax() {
        XCTAssertEqual(calc.total(for: 100), 110, accuracy: 0.001)
    }

    func testNegativeThrows() {
        XCTAssertThrowsError(try calc.validate(-1)) { error in
            XCTAssertEqual(error as? PriceError, .negative)
        }
    }
}
class PriceCalculatorTest {
    private lateinit var calc: PriceCalculator

    @Before fun setUp() { calc = PriceCalculator(0.1) }
    @After fun tearDown() { }

    @Test fun addsTax() = assertEquals(110.0, calc.total(100), 0.001)

    @Test fun negativeThrows() {
        val e = assertThrows(PriceError::class.java) { calc.validate(-1) }
    }
}

Mapping to Swift Testing.

XCTest Swift Testing
class ...: XCTestCase struct/@Suite
func testX() @Test func x()
setUp() / tearDown() init() / deinit
XCTAssertEqual(a, b) #expect(a == b)
XCTUnwrap(x) try #require(x)
XCTAssertThrowsError #expect(throws:)
XCTFail Issue.record
XCTSkip .disabled / .enabled(if:) traits
expectation + wait await confirmation { }
measure { } no equivalent (keep XCTest)
setUpWithError throwing init() throws

Still XCTest-only. UI tests (XCUIApplication), performance tests (measure, XCTMetric), and some attachments/automation. Test plans and coverage work with both.

Lifecycle tip. @MainActor on the test class/suite makes all tests run on the main actor, necessary for testing @MainActor view models and anything touching UIKit.

Real industry examples. Large codebases (Airbnb, Lyft) have tens of thousands of XCTest cases and migrate gradually: new unit tests in Swift Testing, UI tests stay in XCTest. Migration is incremental; both frameworks run in one xcodebuild test.

Everyday analogy. XCTest is a paper exam with fixed formats (class, method naming rules); Swift Testing is a flexible oral exam that still lets old paper exams be graded in the same session.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting the test prefix in XCTest so the method silently never runs.
  • Force-unwrapping var calc: PriceCalculator! and crashing the whole class when setUp fails.
  • Using sleep instead of expectations to wait for async work.
  • Thinking @testable import works on release builds. It needs "Enable Testability", on in Debug, off in Release.

notes.title: Testing async code and actors
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Kotlin you write runTest { } with a TestDispatcher so virtual time makes delay instant. Swift test functions can simply be async; the runner awaits them. There is no virtual time built in, so you inject a clock or avoid real sleeping.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
import Testing

struct ProfileLoaderTests {
    @Test func loadsProfile() async throws {
        let loader = ProfileLoader(api: FakeAPI(result: .success(.stub)))
        let profile = try await loader.load(id: 1)
        #expect(profile.name == "Asha")
    }
}
@Test fun loadsProfile() = runTest {
    val loader = ProfileLoader(FakeApi(Result.success(Profile("Asha"))))
    val profile = loader.load(1)
    assertEquals("Asha", profile.name)
}

Callbacks and events: confirmation. For code that calls a handler N times (old completion-handler APIs, notifications, delegates), use confirmation (Swift Testing) or XCTestExpectation (XCTest).

@Test func notifiesOnce() async {
    await confirmation("handler called", expectedCount: 1) { confirm in
        let service = LegacyService()
        service.fetch { _ in confirm() }
        // wait for completion by bridging, e.g. await a continuation
    }
}
// XCTest form (old codebases)
func testNotifies() {
    let exp = expectation(description: "handler")
    LegacyService().fetch { _ in exp.fulfill() }
    wait(for: [exp], timeout: 2)
}

Note the confirmation closure must finish all confirms before it returns, so wrap callback APIs with withCheckedContinuation to turn them into await.

func fetchAsync(_ s: LegacyService) async -> Data {
    await withCheckedContinuation { cont in
        s.fetch { data in cont.resume(returning: data) }
    }
}

Streams. There is no Turbine; collect from an AsyncStream:

@Test func emitsUpdates() async {
    let (stream, cont) = AsyncStream.makeStream(of: Int.self)
    let model = Counter(source: stream)
    cont.yield(1); cont.yield(2); cont.finish()
    var seen: [Int] = []
    for await v in model.values { seen.append(v) }
    #expect(seen == [1, 2])
}

Actors. Calling an actor's method from a test needs await, which gives you correct isolation for free.

actor Counter { private(set) var n = 0; func inc() { n += 1 } }

@Test func concurrentIncrements() async {
    let c = Counter()
    await withTaskGroup(of: Void.self) { g in
        for _ in 0..<1000 { g.addTask { await c.inc() } }
    }
    #expect(await c.n == 1000)
}

Main actor. Mark the suite @MainActor to test @MainActor types: @MainActor struct HomeViewModelTests { ... }.

Time. Instead of Task.sleep in the code under test, inject a Clock (Swift 5.7+ Clock protocol): production passes ContinuousClock(), tests pass an immediate or manual clock (Point-Free's swift-clocks provides TestClock/ImmediateClock; verify current API). This is the iOS analogue of TestDispatcher.

Swift 6 strictness. Data-race checking errors surface in tests: a non-Sendable fake captured across tasks fails to compile. Make fakes actors or final class ... @unchecked Sendable only with locking, or struct-based.

Real industry examples. Point-Free's swift-concurrency-extras offers withMainSerialExecutor to make async tests deterministic (verify). Apple's docs recommend confirmation over expectations in Swift Testing.

Everyday analogy. Testing async code is waiting for a parcel: await stands at the door until it arrives, while a fake clock lets you fast-forward the delivery time rather than sit through the real days.

Common interview traps.

  • Using Task.sleep to "wait for the result": slow and flaky.
  • Forgetting that XCTestExpectation.wait blocks the thread and can deadlock with main-actor code; prefer await fulfillment(of:).
  • Calling confirm() after the confirmation closure returned.
  • Trying to read an actor property without await.

notes.title: Protocol-based fakes and dependency injection
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. You use Hilt to inject a FakeRepository via @TestInstallIn, or MockK to mock a final class. Swift has no runtime mocking of concrete types, so the idiom is: depend on a protocol (or a closure struct), inject through the initializer, and write a small fake by hand.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
protocol UserRepository: Sendable {
    func user(id: Int) async throws -> User
}

struct LiveUserRepository: UserRepository {
    let client: HTTPClient
    func user(id: Int) async throws -> User { try await client.get("/users/\(id)") }
}

final class FakeUserRepository: UserRepository, @unchecked Sendable {
    private let lock = NSLock()
    private var _calls: [Int] = []
    var result: Result<User, Error> = .success(.stub)

    var calls: [Int] { lock.withLock { _calls } }

    func user(id: Int) async throws -> User {
        lock.withLock { _calls.append(id) }
        return try result.get()
    }
}

@MainActor @Observable
final class ProfileViewModel {
    private let repo: UserRepository
    var state: State = .idle
    enum State: Equatable { case idle, loading, loaded(User), failed(String) }

    init(repo: UserRepository) { self.repo = repo }

    func load(id: Int) async {
        state = .loading
        do { state = .loaded(try await repo.user(id: id)) }
        catch { state = .failed(error.localizedDescription) }
    }
}
interface UserRepository { suspend fun user(id: Int): User }

class FakeUserRepository : UserRepository {
    val calls = mutableListOf<Int>()
    var result: Result<User> = Result.success(User.stub)
    override suspend fun user(id: Int): User { calls += id; return result.getOrThrow() }
}

class ProfileViewModel(private val repo: UserRepository) : ViewModel() {
    val state = MutableStateFlow<State>(State.Idle)
    suspend fun load(id: Int) {
        state.value = State.Loading
        state.value = runCatching { repo.user(id) }
            .fold({ State.Loaded(it) }, { State.Failed(it.message ?: "") })
    }
}

The test:

@MainActor
struct ProfileViewModelTests {
    @Test func loadsUser() async {
        let repo = FakeUserRepository()
        let vm = ProfileViewModel(repo: repo)
        await vm.load(id: 7)
        #expect(vm.state == .loaded(.stub))
        #expect(repo.calls == [7])
    }

    @Test func surfacesFailure() async {
        struct Boom: Error {}
        let repo = FakeUserRepository()
        repo.result = .failure(Boom())
        let vm = ProfileViewModel(repo: repo)
        await vm.load(id: 1)
        guard case .failed = vm.state else { Issue.record("expected failure"); return }
    }
}

Alternatives to protocols.

  • Closure-based clients (struct with var fetch: @Sendable (Int) async throws -> User): trivial to replace in tests, favoured by Point-Free's style.
  • Point-Free swift-dependencies: a @Dependency(\.userRepo) property wrapper with a test-time override (withDependencies). It is the closest iOS analogue to Hilt's test modules. Choose it for large apps.
  • SwiftUI @Environment for view-level injection, and #Preview with fakes.
  • Generics (ProfileViewModel<R: UserRepository>) are faster (static dispatch) but infect type signatures; existential any UserRepository is simpler and fine for I/O-bound deps.

Fake vs mock vs stub. A stub returns canned data, a fake has simplified working logic (in-memory repository), a spy records calls (our calls array), and a mock verifies expectations. Seniors say "fakes plus state assertions" over "interaction verification" because tests stay robust under refactoring.

Real industry examples. Point-Free's Isowords app and the Swift Composable Architecture use swift-dependencies for all effects. Many shops adopt Mockolo (Uber) to generate fakes from protocols (verify current maintenance).

Everyday analogy. A protocol-based fake is a flight simulator: the cockpit (your view model) is real, the sky outside is a stand-in you fully control.

Common interview traps.

  • Injecting a concrete URLSession.shared or a singleton (NetworkManager.shared) and then being unable to test.
  • Making fakes non-Sendable and fighting Swift 6 diagnostics.
  • Over-verifying call order (brittle tests).
  • Forgetting @MainActor isolation on view-model tests.

notes.title: Testing networking with URLProtocol
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. On Android you use OkHttp's MockWebServer to serve canned HTTP responses to the real Retrofit stack. The iOS analogue needs no server: subclass URLProtocol, register it on a URLSessionConfiguration, and intercept every request in-process.

import Foundation

final class MockURLProtocol: URLProtocol, @unchecked Sendable {
    // Test-only global; serialise tests that use it (@Suite(.serialized)).
    nonisolated(unsafe) static var handler: ((URLRequest) throws -> (HTTPURLResponse, Data))?

    override class func canInit(with request: URLRequest) -> Bool { true }
    override class func canonicalRequest(for request: URLRequest) -> URLRequest { request }

    override func startLoading() {
        guard let handler = Self.handler else {
            client?.urlProtocol(self, didFailWithError: URLError(.badServerResponse))
            return
        }
        do {
            let (response, data) = try handler(request)
            client?.urlProtocol(self, didReceive: response, cacheStoragePolicy: .notAllowed)
            client?.urlProtocol(self, didLoad: data)
            client?.urlProtocolDidFinishLoading(self)
        } catch {
            client?.urlProtocol(self, didFailWithError: error)
        }
    }
    override func stopLoading() {}
}

func makeTestSession() -> URLSession {
    let config = URLSessionConfiguration.ephemeral
    config.protocolClasses = [MockURLProtocol.self]
    return URLSession(configuration: config)
}
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
@Suite(.serialized)
struct APIClientTests {
    @Test func decodesUser() async throws {
        MockURLProtocol.handler = { req in
            #expect(req.url?.path == "/users/1")
            let body = #"{"id":1,"name":"Asha"}"#.data(using: .utf8)!
            let resp = HTTPURLResponse(url: req.url!, statusCode: 200,
                                       httpVersion: nil, headerFields: nil)!
            return (resp, body)
        }
        let client = APIClient(session: makeTestSession(), baseURL: URL(string: "https://x.test")!)
        let user: User = try await client.get("/users/1")
        #expect(user.name == "Asha")
    }

    @Test func mapsServerErrors() async {
        MockURLProtocol.handler = { req in
            (HTTPURLResponse(url: req.url!, statusCode: 500, httpVersion: nil, headerFields: nil)!, Data())
        }
        let client = APIClient(session: makeTestSession(), baseURL: URL(string: "https://x.test")!)
        await #expect(throws: APIError.server(500)) {
            let _: User = try await client.get("/users/1")
        }
    }
}
class ApiClientTest {
    private val server = MockWebServer()

    @Test fun decodesUser() = runTest {
        server.enqueue(MockResponse().setBody("""{"id":1,"name":"Asha"}"""))
        server.start()
        val api = Retrofit.Builder().baseUrl(server.url("/"))
            .addConverterFactory(MoshiConverterFactory.create()).build()
            .create(UserApi::class.java)
        assertEquals("Asha", api.user(1).name)
        assertEquals("/users/1", server.takeRequest().path)
    }
}

Details.

  • Production code must accept an injected URLSession, not use URLSession.shared. This is the single design decision that makes networking testable.
  • ephemeral configuration avoids disk cache and cookies contaminating tests.
  • Request bodies: URLProtocol receives httpBodyStream, not httpBody, for upload requests; read the stream if you need to assert on the body (a frequent gotcha).
  • Decoding tests: keep JSON fixtures as files in the test bundle and load with Bundle(for:) or Swift Testing's Bundle.module for packages.
  • Libraries: OHHTTPStubs (old, popular), Mocker, and swift-snapshot-testing for recording. All build on URLProtocol.

Real industry examples. Alamofire's own test suite and many Apple sample apps use URLProtocol stubs. Spotify-scale apps often add a record/replay layer (like VCR) to capture real traffic once.

Everyday analogy. URLProtocol is a postal sorter that intercepts your letters before they leave the building and hands back a pre-written reply, so you can practise correspondence without ever touching the real post.

Common interview traps.

  • Registering URLProtocol.registerClass globally and leaking stubs between tests (parallel tests break). Prefer per-session protocolClasses.
  • Static mutable handlers in parallel tests: mark the suite .serialized.
  • Reading request.httpBody and getting nil for POSTs.
  • Hitting the real network in unit tests.

notes.title: Testing view models and SwiftUI state
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. For a ViewModel exposing StateFlow you test with runTest and collect state. With @Observable view models in SwiftUI there is no Flow to collect; you call methods and read properties. The Android UI (Compose) is tested by rule; SwiftUI has no first-party view-introspection test API, so you keep logic out of views and test view models.

@MainActor @Observable
final class SearchViewModel {
    private let search: @Sendable (String) async throws -> [Item]
    var query = ""
    var results: [Item] = []
    var isLoading = false

    init(search: @escaping @Sendable (String) async throws -> [Item]) { self.search = search }

    func submit() async {
        isLoading = true
        defer { isLoading = false }
        results = (try? await search(query)) ?? []
    }
}

@MainActor
struct SearchViewModelTests {
    @Test func submitPopulatesResults() async {
        let vm = SearchViewModel(search: { _ in [.stub] })
        vm.query = "x"
        await vm.submit()
        #expect(vm.results.count == 1)
        #expect(vm.isLoading == false)
    }
}

Observing intermediate states. Because submit suspends, to assert isLoading == true mid-flight use a gate (a continuation or AsyncStream) in the fake rather than sleeping. Or use Observation's withObservationTracking (confirm semantics: verify) or Point-Free's Observation helpers.

Combine-based old code (@Published): test with sink into an array plus XCTestExpectation, or .values async sequence (bridging publisher to AsyncSequence).

Architectures and testability. MVVM with protocol dependencies is the baseline. The Composable Architecture's TestStore asserts every state change and effect exhaustively: await store.send(.buttonTapped) { $0.count = 1 } fails if the closure does not match the real state change. It is stricter than plain view-model tests.

Real industry examples. Airbnb and many fintech apps keep views dumb and test view models; Point-Free open-sourced the TestStore approach and uses it throughout its apps.

Everyday analogy. Testing a view model is rehearsing a play without the stage lights: all the actors' lines and cues are checked, and only the final look (pixels) is left to a visual check.

Common interview traps.

  • Putting business logic inside View.body or .task closures, which cannot be unit-tested.
  • Forgetting @MainActor, getting Swift 6 errors on property access from a nonisolated test.
  • Asserting only the end state of an async flow and missing the loading transitions.
  • Testing SwiftUI by reflection hacks (ViewInspector) as the primary strategy; it is a last resort (verify library status).

notes.title: Snapshot testing and previews as tests
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Paparazzi/Roborazzi render Compose to a PNG on the JVM and diff against a golden image; Compose previews can double as screenshot tests. iOS uses swift-snapshot-testing (Point-Free) and, optionally, previews.

import SnapshotTesting
import SwiftUI
import XCTest

final class ProfileCardSnapshotTests: XCTestCase {
    func testProfileCard() {
        let view = ProfileCard(user: .stub).frame(width: 320)
        let host = UIHostingController(rootView: view)
        assertSnapshot(of: host, as: .image(on: .iPhone13))
        // record = true (or SNAPSHOT_TESTING_RECORD env) re-records goldens
    }
}

How it works. The first run writes a reference image under __Snapshots__; later runs render again and compare pixels (with precision and perceptualPrecision tolerances). Dark mode and Dynamic Type variants are added with traits: (e.g., .image(on: .iPhone13, traits: .init(userInterfaceStyle: .dark))). Swift Testing support exists in newer versions of the library (verify).

Pitfalls.

  • Rendering differs across Xcode/iOS versions and simulator models; pin the Simulator device and OS in CI. Anti-aliasing and font differences cause false diffs, which is why perceptualPrecision (e.g., 0.98) exists.
  • Commit goldens to git; large PNG churn bloats the repo (use Git LFS if needed).
  • Animations and async images make snapshots flaky; inject static data and disable animations.

Previews as tests. #Preview is a development tool, not a test, but teams treat the set of previews as a gallery and some tools turn them into snapshots (e.g., PreviewSnapshots, Point-Free's helpers, or Apple's Xcode 16 previews in a test target; verify). Cheap value: build previews for loading, error, empty, long text, large Dynamic Type, dark mode and RTL, and run snapshots against them.

Real industry examples. Airbnb publishes a snapshot-heavy approach for its design system; Lyft, Uber and Pinterest run large snapshot suites. Kickstarter open-sourced the idea for its iOS app.

Everyday analogy. A snapshot test is "spot the difference" between yesterday's photo of the shop window and today's; any change in the display is flagged for you to approve or fix.

Common interview traps.

  • Recording snapshots on a developer's laptop and verifying on a CI machine with a different simulator, causing permanent failures.
  • Re-recording blindly to make tests pass (defeats the purpose).
  • Using snapshots instead of logic tests; they check appearance, not behaviour.
  • Treating #Preview as an automatic regression test; it is not one by itself.

notes.title: XCUITest, accessibility identifiers and Espresso comparison
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Espresso (View) and createComposeRule (Compose) run in-process and find nodes by id, text or testTag. XCUITest runs out of process via the accessibility layer: it sees the UI as an accessibility tree and sends synthetic events. You can only query what accessibility exposes.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
import XCTest

final class LoginUITests: XCTestCase {
    override func setUpWithError() throws {
        continueAfterFailure = false
    }

    @MainActor
    func testLoginShowsHome() throws {
        let app = XCUIApplication()
        app.launchArguments += ["-uiTesting"]
        app.launchEnvironment["API_BASE"] = "http://localhost:8080"
        app.launch()

        let email = app.textFields["login.email"]
        XCTAssertTrue(email.waitForExistence(timeout: 5))
        email.tap()
        email.typeText("asha@example.com")

        app.secureTextFields["login.password"].tap()
        app.secureTextFields["login.password"].typeText("hunter2")
        app.buttons["login.submit"].tap()

        XCTAssertTrue(app.staticTexts["home.title"].waitForExistence(timeout: 5))
    }
}
@get:Rule val rule = createAndroidComposeRule<MainActivity>()

@Test fun loginShowsHome() {
    rule.onNodeWithTag("login.email").performTextInput("asha@example.com")
    rule.onNodeWithTag("login.password").performTextInput("hunter2")
    rule.onNodeWithTag("login.submit").performClick()
    rule.onNodeWithTag("home.title").assertIsDisplayed()
}

Accessibility identifiers. The iOS equivalent of testTag is accessibilityIdentifier. It is invisible to users (unlike accessibilityLabel, which VoiceOver reads and which is localised) and does not hurt accessibility.

TextField("Email", text: $email)
    .accessibilityIdentifier("login.email")
Button("Sign in", action: submit)
    .accessibilityIdentifier("login.submit")

Never query by visible text: it breaks with localisation. A gotcha: applying .accessibilityIdentifier on a container can override children's identifiers in SwiftUI; use .accessibilityElement(children: .contain) where needed (verify behaviour per iOS version).

Stability tactics.

  • Use waitForExistence(timeout:) and XCTNSPredicateExpectation instead of sleep. XCUITest auto-waits for the app to be idle (animations, runloop), but not for network.
  • Drive the app into a known state with launchArguments / launchEnvironment (read in App.init): swap in a fake backend, skip onboarding, reset the store, disable animations (UIView.setAnimationsEnabled(false)).
  • Page-object pattern: wrap each screen in a struct exposing actions.
  • Handle system alerts with addUIInterruptionMonitor, or reset permissions per run with app.resetAuthorizationStatus(for: .camera).
  • Keep the count low (critical user journeys); each takes seconds to tens of seconds because the app launches fresh.

Records and tools. Xcode can record interactions (Record button) to bootstrap code, though the output needs cleanup. Test run results with screenshots and videos go into the .xcresult bundle; attach them on failure with XCTAttachment. Third parties: Maestro, Appium and EarlGrey (Google, now less active; verify) exist but XCUITest remains the default.

Real industry examples. Airbnb, Spotify and Wikipedia's iOS app all use XCUITest for smoke journeys. Many teams run UI tests against a local mock server (Swifter, GCDWebServer, or a Vapor stub) for determinism.

Everyday analogy. XCUITest is a mystery shopper: she can only interact with the shop the way a customer does, via shelf labels (identifiers), and cannot peek into the stockroom.

Common interview traps.

  • Querying by label text, which is localised.
  • Using sleep(5) instead of waiting for an element.
  • Expecting to access app internals or mock classes from the UI test target (separate process).
  • Putting identifiers on SwiftUI containers and overriding child identifiers.

notes.title: Test plans, coverage and flaky tests
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Gradle you configure test tasks, build variants and Jacoco, and shard on CI (Firebase Test Lab matrix). Xcode uses test plans (.xctestplan, JSON) that define which test targets run, in which configurations (language, region, dark mode), with what environment variables, and whether code coverage, parallelisation and repetition are on.

{
  "configurations": [
    { "name": "English / Light", "options": { "language": "en", "region": "US" } },
    { "name": "German / Dark",   "options": { "language": "de", "userInterfaceStyle": "dark" } }
  ],
  "defaultOptions": {
    "codeCoverage": true,
    "testExecutionOrdering": "random",
    "environmentVariableEntries": [ { "key": "UITEST", "value": "1" } ]
  },
  "testTargets": [
    { "target": { "name": "MyAppTests" } },
    { "target": { "name": "MyAppUITests" }, "skippedTests": ["SlowTests"] }
  ],
  "version": 1
}

(Shape is approximate; the file is edited in Xcode's UI and its exact keys: verify.)

Common plans: a Unit plan for every PR (fast), a UI plan for merge/nightly, and a Localisation plan running the same UI tests in several languages. Run them with:

xcodebuild test \
  -scheme MyApp \
  -testPlan Unit \
  -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 15,OS=17.5' \
  -resultBundlePath build/Unit.xcresult \
  -enableCodeCoverage YES

Parallelism. -parallel-testing-enabled YES clones simulators and runs test classes in parallel (XCTest); Swift Testing additionally parallelises inside a process. This is why shared mutable state is the number one source of test pollution.

Coverage. Xcode reports line coverage per target and file; export from the .xcresult with xcrun xccov view --report build/Unit.xcresult. Use it to find untested code, not as a target to maximise. Teams typically gate on coverage of changed lines, with tools like Codecov or Danger. Be careful that UI tests inflate coverage numbers with incidental execution.

Flaky tests. Causes: real time/sleep, shared singletons, test order dependence, network, animations, simulator state, race conditions. Defences:

  • Randomised order in test plans exposes dependence.
  • Repetition: "Test Repetitions" with "Retry on failure" (Xcode 13+) runs failures again; -test-iterations 10 -run-tests-until-failure for hunting.
  • Quarantine: tag flaky tests, skip in the blocking plan, track a ticket.
  • Fresh simulator per run (xcrun simctl erase all), pinned OS version.
  • Inject clocks, schedulers and network fakes.

CI. GitHub Actions on macos-14/macos-15 runners (macOS runners are costly and slower than Linux), Xcode Cloud, Bitrise, or self-hosted Mac minis. Cache Swift Package Manager (~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData / .build) and use xcbeautify for readable logs. See the signing/CI note in this track for pipeline specifics.

Real industry examples. Uber and Lyft shard their UI tests across many simulators and quarantine flaky ones automatically; Spotify has publicly discussed flaky-test dashboards. Apple's xcresulttool lets you parse failures into reports.

Everyday analogy. A test plan is a flight checklist variant (day, night, storm); coverage is how many switches in the cockpit you at least touched; flaky tests are a smoke alarm that sometimes beeps with no smoke, which teaches the crew to ignore real alarms.

Common interview traps.

  • Chasing 100% coverage with assertion-free tests.
  • Auto-retrying flaky tests forever instead of fixing root causes.
  • Different simulator OS locally and on CI.
  • Forgetting that xcodebuild test needs a booted or bootable destination and a shared scheme checked into git.

notes.title: Performance tests and what to test first
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Android has Macrobenchmark and Microbenchmark for performance. iOS has measure blocks in XCTest, XCTMetric types (XCTClockMetric, XCTCPUMetric, XCTMemoryMetric, XCTApplicationLaunchMetric, XCTOSSignpostMetric), and Instruments for profiling.

final class SortPerfTests: XCTestCase {
    func testSortPerformance() {
        let data = (0..<100_000).map { _ in Int.random(in: 0..<1_000_000) }
        measure(metrics: [XCTClockMetric(), XCTMemoryMetric()]) {
            _ = data.sorted()
        }
    }

    @MainActor
    func testLaunchPerformance() throws {
        measure(metrics: [XCTApplicationLaunchMetric()]) {
            XCUIApplication().launch()
        }
    }
}

Xcode stores a baseline per device and fails when the result regresses beyond a tolerance (default relative standard deviation 10%; baselines are device-specific, so run on pinned CI hardware). Use os_signpost intervals and XCTOSSignpostMetric to measure real user flows such as scroll hitches. Instruments (Time Profiler, Allocations, Hangs) is for diagnosis; MetricKit and Xcode Organizer give production numbers (launch time, hang rate).

What to test first, a senior's ordering.

  1. Pure business logic and mappers (fast, highest value).
  2. View models with fakes: state transitions, error paths.
  3. Networking decode/encode and error mapping via URLProtocol.
  4. Persistence with an in-memory SwiftData ModelConfiguration(isStoredInMemoryOnly: true) or an in-memory Core Data store (old code).
  5. A small set of UI journeys: launch, login, purchase, deep link.
  6. Snapshots for the design system components.
import SwiftData
import Testing

@MainActor
struct StoreTests {
    @Test func savesNote() throws {
        let container = try ModelContainer(
            for: Note.self,
            configurations: ModelConfiguration(isStoredInMemoryOnly: true))
        let ctx = container.mainContext
        ctx.insert(Note(title: "hi"))
        try ctx.save()
        #expect(try ctx.fetch(FetchDescriptor<Note>()).count == 1)
    }
}

Test-friendly design habits. Inject everything (clock, UUID generator, date provider, URLSession, UserDefaults suite via UserDefaults(suiteName: UUID().uuidString)), avoid singletons, mark types Sendable, keep side effects behind protocols. Use a fresh UserDefaults suite per test to avoid cross-test pollution.

Real industry examples. Apple's performance guidance and WWDC sessions on hitches use XCTHitchMetric (verify name) for scrolling; Meta and Spotify track launch time per release in dashboards fed by MetricKit.

Everyday analogy. Performance tests are the stopwatch at a track meet: only meaningful if you run on the same track (device) in the same conditions every time.

Common interview traps.

  • Comparing measure baselines across different machines.
  • Testing persistence against the real on-disk store, leaking data between tests.
  • Using UserDefaults.standard in tests, so state bleeds across runs.
  • Measuring in Debug builds (unoptimised); performance tests should use a Release-like configuration.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Default to Swift Testing for unit tests (@Test, #expect, #require, traits, parameterised arguments, fresh suite instance per test, parallel by default); keep XCTest for UI, performance and old code.
  • Test async code by making the test async; use confirmation for callbacks, AsyncStream for streams, and an injected Clock instead of sleeping; mark view-model suites @MainActor.
  • There is no runtime mocking in Swift: depend on protocols or closure structs, inject via initialisers (or swift-dependencies), and write fakes and spies by hand, Sendable-safe for Swift 6.
  • Test networking by injecting a URLSession configured with a URLProtocol stub (iOS's MockWebServer); beware httpBodyStream and global handlers in parallel tests.
  • Keep logic out of SwiftUI views and test @Observable view models; use snapshot tests (pinned simulator, perceptual precision) for appearance.
  • XCUITest runs out of process through the accessibility tree: use accessibilityIdentifier (the testTag), waitForExistence, launch arguments to control state, and few journeys.
  • Use test plans for unit versus UI versus localisation configurations, measure coverage via .xcresult, and attack flakiness with random order, retries as a diagnostic, injected time and pinned simulators.
